The instrument is held upright, between the knees or resting on the legs, and sounded by drawing a bow across the strings; the bow is held underhand. The fingerboard is fretted, and the strings are stopped against the frets. Six strings are usual, tuned mostly in fourths with one major third in the middle; a beginner can first get to know this tuning and the finger positions, then practise coordinating the hold on the instrument, the bow grip and the stopped fingers.
低音維奧爾琴於十五世紀末在西班牙瓦倫西亞一帶成形，與可用手指、撥片或弓演奏的維烏: The viola da gamba took shape around Valencia in Spain at the end of the fifteenth century, connected with the vihuela, which could be played with the fingers, a plectrum or a bow, and it then passed into Italy and the rest of Europe. It went on developing in sixteenth-century Italy, where treble, alto, bass and other sizes appeared, and in the Renaissance and Baroque it was widely used for solo playing, consorts and basso continuo. In the late seventeenth century, being less loud than the violin family, it lost favour in larger halls, and the cello and double bass took over some of its work. It was revived in the twentieth century with the period-instrument movement, to restore the sound of early music.
低音維奧爾琴音色溫潤深沉，帶有獨特的蒼涼感與內斂的表現力。其音域寬廣，特別在中低: The viola da gamba has a warm, deep timbre, with a sadness of its own and an inward kind of expressiveness. Its range is wide, and in the middle and low registers especially it has a full, forgiving tone. The horsehair bow and the several strings give the resonance many layers and produce a warm sound with a slight huskiness. Beside the bright directness of the modern cello, the gamba sounds more antique and more distant; beside older viols its bass is deeper and more forceful. The particular shape of the resonating body lets the sound waves die away naturally, leaving a graceful tail. The instrument is especially suited to the quiet substance of Baroque music: its tone can set out deep feeling on its own, and it also blends perfectly with voices, making a plain and refined musical world.

The viola da gamba (also called the viol) is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71, and a fretted, bowed member of the viol family. Most have six gut strings, tuned mainly in fourths with a third in the middle; the instrument is held between the knees or on the legs, and the bow is held underhand. Unlike the violin family it has movable frets, a flat back and sloping shoulders. In the art music of Renaissance and Baroque Europe it was used for solo playing, consorts and basso continuo, and came in treble, alto and bass sizes among others.
琴身早期以平直木板拼合，部分後期有雕刻面板；側板早期淺，後加深。發聲體為弦，屬弦: Early bodies were built up from flat boards, and some later ones have a carved front; the ribs were shallow at first and became deeper. The sounding body is the string, the instrument is a chordophone, and the region is Europe / Spain. The strings are gut, at low tension; in later instruments the lowest string could be gut, or a silk core wound with copper, and there are also strings of copper wire wound into gut fibre. The frets are movable, tied-on gut frets. Traditionally the parts are glued with animal glue, and the inner joints are reinforced with linen or parchment dipped in hot animal glue. The pegbox at the head may be carved with an animal, a human head or a scroll. Early instruments have no soundpost, and the bridge, flat at first, later became a wide arch. The other woods are not recorded.
